title: Porous, semi-porous and hard material decisions
audience: Supervisors, coordinators and trained cleaners who may be asked to triage, refer or document mould-related work in homes, rentals and commercial buildings, under an approved plan. Not a qualification or authority to remediate, demolish, or certify any building or room.
learningOutcomes: Classify described items as hard, semi-porous or porous.
Refuse to keep a porous item on appearance alone.
Record each material decision and its referral.

instruction.heading: Scope of this lesson
instruction.body: This lesson covers recognising material types and referring decisions about them. It does not decide that a porous item can be cleaned, and it does not authorise demolition or salvage.

instruction.heading: What the guideline says
instruction.body: The WA Department of Health guideline says porous items that cannot be adequately cleaned should be removed or discarded in simple remediation, and that such items are often not economically salvageable as part of typical remediation. For hard surfaces it advises scrubbing with soapy water, and it says the physical action of scrubbing is the most important component. It also says that chemical products may be used in some cases, but will not fully remove mould, and that their use is a case-specific decision. Hard surfaces are therefore cleaned by the approved method, and porous items are judged against whether they can be adequately cleaned.

instruction.heading: Decisions in practice
instruction.body: Saturated drywall and timber beside washable metal fixtures need different decisions. Porous material that has held moisture and growth is judged for salvage by the competent supervisor. Mark each item as hard, semi-porous or porous, record its condition and any uncertainty, and refer the decision. Do not decide that an item is safe to keep because it looks clean. Looks clean is an observation, not a result of cleaning.

procedure: Classify each item as hard, semi-porous or porous, and record its condition.
For hard surfaces, use the approved cleaning method and nothing beyond it.
For porous items, record whether they can be adequately cleaned, and refer the decision.
Mark items that cannot be adequately cleaned for removal or discard, as the plan directs.
Keep a register of decisions, and do not keep an item because it looks clean.
Record the referral and the decision maker.

workedExamples.situation: Saturated plasterboard sits beside a washable metal fixture in the same bathroom.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the decision for each?
workedExamples.reasoning: The plasterboard is porous and has been saturated, so its salvage is a competent supervisor's decision. The metal fixture is hard and can be cleaned under the approved method. Record each item separately.

workedExamples.situation: A fabric sofa looks clean after surface wiping, but smells musty.
workedExamples.reasoning: Not on appearance. Record the odour and the uncertainty about the interior, and refer for a competent decision. The guideline states that porous items that cannot be adequately cleaned should be removed or discarded.

equipmentAndPpe: Material classification register with fields for type, condition and uncertainty.
Training-only mock material cards. No real material is cleaned or removed in this lesson.

commonErrors.error: Keeping porous items because they look clean.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the uncertainty, and refer for a decision on whether the item can be adequately cleaned.

commonErrors.error: Applying one cleaning method to every material.
commonErrors.prevention: Classify each material and use the method the plan gives for it.

commonErrors.error: Using a chemical product as a blanket fix.
commonErrors.prevention: Treat chemical use as a case-specific decision in the approved plan.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Decisions to salvage, demolish or discard building materials are for the competent supervisor, under the approved plan.
The porous-item statements come from the WA guideline. Disposal of removed material depends on local rules.

qualityStandard: The learner classifies described items as hard, semi-porous or porous.
The learner refuses to keep a porous item on appearance alone.
The learner records each decision and its referral.
documentationEvidence: Material classification register with condition and uncertainty.
Decision record for each porous item, with the decision maker.
summary: Hard surfaces are cleaned by the plan's method.
Porous items that cannot be adequately cleaned are removed or discarded.
Looks clean is not a decision.

knowledgeChecks.question: A porous item looks clean but smells musty. What is correct?
options: Keep it, because it looks clean.
Wipe it again and keep it.
Record the odour and uncertainty and refer the decision, since it may not be adequately cleanable.

knowledgeChecks.question: What does the WA guideline say about porous items that cannot be adequately cleaned?
options: They should be removed or discarded.
They must be painted to seal them.
They can be kept if they are in a sunny room.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which material is a hard surface for the purpose of this lesson?
options: A timber shelf with a soft finish.

sourceReferences: Internal draft: curriculum/courses/high-risk/HR04-mould-remediation.json, section 8 (reworded; no source text copied).

WA Department of Health, Guidelines for managing mould and dampness, April 2024 edition, sections 3.2.2 and 4.2.2, read 2026-11-03 through a page-summary tool. Appendix D (damp and water-damaged materials) was listed in the contents but its text was not read.

officialReferences.title: Guidelines for managing mould and dampness: related public health risks in buildings (WA Department of Health)
officialReferences.pageDate: April 2024 (version control table); publication code ENV-0014702 MAY'24; no separate last-updated date shown
officialReferences.covers: Read through a page-summary tool on 2026-11-03 (PDF, Environmental Health Directorate, WA Department of Health). Section 1.4 sets out a general public health duty, a workplace duty and a residential tenancies duty. Section 2.1 names people with existing respiratory, immunocompromising and allergic conditions, and infants, children and older people. Section 3.2.2 says porous items are often not economically salvageable and must be thrown out. Section 3.3 says the source must be located to address the cause and prevent recurrence. Section 3.4.1 defines simple contamination as new, isolated and visible, no greater than one square metre, with easily identified causes, and its footnote calls the one-square-metre size arbitrary. Section 3.4.2 defines complex contamination as larger than one square metre or found in multiple rooms or places. Section 3.5 states there are no defined quantitative or qualitative exposure thresholds for mould or dampness. Section 4.1 lists containment, drying and source repair as principles. Section 4.2.2 advises scrubbing hard surfaces with soapy water, avoiding dry brushing, cleaning at least 30 to 50 cm beyond the visible mould, removing or discarding porous items that cannot be adequately cleaned, stating that mould is not considered hazardous waste, and not painting, sealing or covering surfaces until dry. Section 4.3 recommends a site-specific plan with professionals for complex contamination, isolation with heavy grade plastic and negative pressure, and evacuation of occupants. Section 4.4 lists no recurrence within two to four weeks after remediation as an indicator of success, recommends the evaluation be done by a different entity, and states there are no legal requirements for a post-remediation assessment. Appendix B recommends a P2 or N95 respirator and says PAPRs should be used for complex remediation. Appendix E says mould can grow within 24 to 48 hours in flood-affected homes.

moduleAuthority.heading: Module authority and restricted work
moduleAuthority.body: This module is training content. It does not grant authority to remediate, demolish, disturb building materials, handle contaminated water or waste, or certify that a building, room or occupant area is safe or free of mould or pathogens. Completing this lesson does not give a licence, certificate or approval. Restricted or high-exposure remediation is carried out only by an appropriately qualified and competent professional under an approved plan, and some related work, including asbestos and lead disturbance and certain waste handling, is restricted to licensed or specially authorised people. The owner, manager, tenant or contract may define what work is permitted, but where the contract covers only routine cleaning, that is the limit of the task. Where the controlling authority or the competent supervisor is not identified, stop and refer.

stopWorkAndReferral.heading: Stop-work and referral rules for this module
stopWorkAndReferral.body: Stop and refer whenever any of these is true: the hazards are unknown or changing; the work is destructive or hazardous and outside the authorised scope; exposure is uncontrolled or the building is unsafe to occupy; supervision, equipment or permissions are insufficient; flood, sewage, asbestos or lead may be present; a worker's PPE or respirator readiness has not been verified; a client asks for a clearance or pathogen-free statement; or a waste route is unauthorised. A stop-work decision is correct. Record it and restart only after the competent supervisor has confirmed the scope in writing.
